item.title: Chinese partnership helps Spain strengthen EV value chain
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
The new partnership aims to make Sagunto a European production hub for LFP-based Unified Cells. The plant's first phase is now planned at up to 30 GWh of annual capacity, 50 percent above the 20 GWh initially considered. MADRID, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Spain builds more than 2 million vehicles a year as Europe's second-largest vehicle producer, but many decisions shaping its automotive industry are made abroad. With Volkswagen considering a possible phase-out of its Spanish brand SEAT after 2030, a new battery partnership with China's Gotion High-Tech highlights Spain's efforts to secure its place in the electric-vehicle value chain. Volkswagen Group, its battery unit PowerCo and Gotion announced on Sept. 28 that Gotion will invest around 1.1 billion euros (1.29 billion U.S. dollars) for a 49-percent stake in PowerCo's battery-cell plant in Sagunto, eastern Spain. PowerCo will retain 51 percent, with the venture intended to be jointly managed and operations to start in 2027. Jose Diez, second vice president of the Valencian regional government, said the partnership would combine "industrial experience and technological knowledge" to make the project more competitive. A POWERHOUSE WITH LIMITED CONTROL Spain has an extensive automotive manufacturing ecosystem spanning assembly plants, component makers and supplier network. According to ICEX, Spain's state export and investment agency, nine multinational groups operate 18 vehicle assembly and component plants in the country. The broader automotive industry accounts for around 10 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and 16 percent of goods exports. Yet much of that industrial strength sits within multinational groups, leaving Spain exposed to investment and production decisions made elsewhere. Uncertainty over SEAT has brought that vulnerability into focus. In September, Volkswagen said tighter CO2 rules, electrification costs and the investment needed for a new generation of electric models were making further investment in the brand increasingly complex. Volkswagen's options beyond 2030 include a gradual phase-out. The announcement has stirred concerns in Spain. El Pais reported that SEAT's direct and indirect economic footprint is estimated at around 4 percent of Catalonia's GDP and 3 percent of employment. Matias Carnero, president of SEAT's works council and currently a member of Volkswagen's supervisory board, has warned against allowing SEAT to become "a mere assembly plant." He told Catalan newspaper La Vanguardia that SEAT still retains activities spanning design, production and sales. "The whole value chain - that is what matters," he said. WHY CHINESE TECHNOLOGY MATTERS Electrification is changing what gives automotive manufacturers a competitive edge. "It is no longer just about who manufactures better, but who controls batteries, software, costs and the speed of innovation," Xavier Ferre, partner responsible for automotive and transport at EY Spain, told local media La Vanguardia. Batteries illustrate that shift. According to Volkswagen, Europe still lacks significant industrial-scale production capacity for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, a technology increasingly used in lower-cost mass-market electric vehicles. Gotion brings established expertise in LFP technology and large-scale manufacturing. The new partnership aims to make Sagunto a European production hub for LFP-based Unified Cells. The plant's first phase is now planned at up to 30 GWh of annual capacity, 50 percent above the 20 GWh initially considered. The cells are intended to feed Volkswagen Group's electric-vehicle production network in Spain, including small electric models assembled at SEAT's Martorell plant in Catalonia and Volkswagen Navarra. Another major project is taking shape in Zaragoza, where Stellantis and China's CATL are investing up to 4.1 billion euros (4.62 billion dollars) in a 50-50 joint venture to build an LFP battery plant with a capacity of up to 50 GWh. Construction began in 2025, and production is scheduled to start by the end of 2026. Such projects could help Spain anchor battery manufacturing alongside vehicle assembly, strengthening its position as production shifts toward electric models. FROM COMPETITION TO INDUSTRIAL COOPERATION Spain's partnerships with Chinese companies extend beyond batteries. Chery has partnered with Spanish brand Ebro to revive production at Nissan's former Barcelona plant. Ford and Geely have agreed to form a joint venture around the Almussafes plant in Valencia, pending regulatory approval. Stellantis is also deepening industrial cooperation with Leapmotor, with production planned in Zaragoza. These alliances offer ways to sustain factories and supplier networks while attracting new technology and investment. Battery investment is pushing localization further upstream. Gotion's separate project in Valladolid includes cathode production and advanced battery recycling, adding activities beyond vehicle assembly. When the project was announced in July, the Spanish government described it as a "historic opportunity" to strengthen the country's electric-vehicle industrial base, with thousands of jobs expected to be created. Josep Maria Vall, president of the Catalan Automotive Industry Cluster (CIAC), said Spain's manufacturing history and experienced component makers give it the capacity to integrate Chinese manufacturers into its industrial ecosystem. CIAC Manager Josep Nadal said deeper investment and industrial alliances could help Europe "retain the value chain." Pablo Sanz, a professor at Spain's National University of Distance Education, told Xinhua that Chinese brands are pushing European companies to improve quality, accelerate innovation and increase efficiency. "Spain and Europe need Chinese brands to accelerate innovation," he said. Jaume Roura, president of Catalonia's Fecavem vehicle dealers' association, told Xinhua that cooperation should deliver benefits on both sides. "We must make sure everyone benefits and, above all, that industry and jobs are maintained," he said.

item.title: China's cat parks seek lasting, sustainable homes for strays
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
CHONGQING/HARBIN, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- When Chongqing Firefly Bay Cat Harbor Park opened on New Year's Day in southwest China, it had just over 600 cats. More than eight months later, the number has passed 1,000. By September, the 30,000-square-meter riverside park had rescued or taken in more than 1,300 cats, while over 240 had been adopted. As the number of cats grows, so do the demands on the park -- from veterinary care and staffing to finding enough space for new arrivals. "The first thing is to keep the daily operation running," said Jian Ning, who oversees offline operations at the park. "We have to survive first before talking about anything else." The park sits on what was a long-idle site near Nanbin Road in Chongqing Municipality. The local government provides the land rent-free, while the operator earns revenue from admission fees, spending inside the park and rent paid by businesses on the site. A ticket costs 19.9 yuan (about 3 U.S. dollars). During the city's hot summer, when fewer people visit the outdoor park, daily attendance averages just over 300. On its busiest day, however, the park received 8,000 visitors. Veterinary care accounts for roughly one-third of operating costs, Jian said. Current revenue is enough to keep the park running day to day, but making a profit remains difficult. "If we had to pay normal rent, the operating pressure would be much greater," Jian said. The park now employs 51 people, including animal-care staff, security guards and cleaners. Most employees who work directly with the cats are in their 20s. All are paid, full-time staff. "We don't expect people to work simply for love," Jian said. Most members of the park's core team are from stray-cat rescue groups. They had seen rescue efforts struggle with a basic problem: expenses kept mounting, while funding often depended on donations, subsidies or rescuers paying out of their own pockets. The team therefore decided to open the site to visitors, hoping revenue from ticket sales and other businesses could help cover the cost of long-term care for rescued cats. The park sums up the idea in a lighthearted slogan: "Cats work to support themselves." The experiment is unfolding alongside a sizable pet economy. China had 126 million pet dogs and cats in urban areas in 2025, including 72.89 million cats, while the urban dog-and-cat consumer market reached 312.6 billion yuan, according to the 2026 China Pet Industry White Paper (Consumption Report). Yet space has a limit. Jian estimated that the park could accommodate 2,000 to 3,000 cats. If the population approaches that level, she said, new admissions will have to be reduced. The park does not encourage people to relocate stray cats that are regularly fed in residential communities, as they have already grown accustomed to those surroundings, Jian said. Scientific research also suggests that managing free-roaming cat populations requires more than one-off interventions. A 12-year controlled study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that sustained, high-intensity neutering across contiguous areas could reduce cat numbers, while immigration and other compensatory effects could weaken the impact. The researchers recommended combining the trap-neuter-return method with complementary measures such as adoption and resource management. Adoption certainly provides another outlet. Applicants face strict requirements, however, and the park conducts follow-up checks. None of the more than 240 adopted cats have so far been returned. Visitors, meanwhile, must adapt to rules designed around the animals. Children under six are not admitted, and staff ask visitors not to chase cats or pick them up against their will. Jian said disputes over scratches and bites have become less common as visitor guidance has improved. The park may stop admitting visitors once more than 3,000 people are inside. So far, the flow of people in and out has made that unnecessary. Some 3,000 kilometers away in northeast China, another cat park is testing a similar combination of animal rescue and tourism on a smaller scale. Scarlett's Friends, Heilongjiang Province's first cat-themed park, opened on Aug. 28 at the Yabuli Ski Resort in Harbin and is now home to 150 rescued stray cats. The cat park occupies a site that had stood idle for years and gives Yabuli, long known for winter skiing, another attraction for the warmer months. Before entering areas open to visitors, the cats must be neutered, vaccinated, treated for parasites, and assessed to determine whether they can adapt to interaction with people. Sick cats are moved to an isolation area, while a partner veterinary hospital provides regular health support. Winter in Yabuli brings temperatures far below freezing. Indoor activity areas and cat houses have been equipped with air-source heating systems, and the cats will spend most of the winter indoors, said Liu Guangpeng, deputy general manager of Harbin Yabuli Tourism Investment Group Co., Ltd. Ning Xiaofeng, general manager of the group, said stray-cat rescue that relies solely on continued spending is difficult to sustain. By linking the park with tourism, the operator aims to use tourism revenue to help cover the cost of caring for the cats while providing them with a stable home. Liu said the park would limit visitor numbers rather than compromise the cats' welfare. "Even if there were no visitors, we would still make sure the cats were properly cared for," he said. If crowds exceeded the park's capacity, it would introduce reservations and limit entry. Similar ideas have begun to appear in local policies. In February, the eastern Chinese city of Nanjing in Jiangsu Province issued guidelines encouraging pet-related tourism while calling for stray animals to be managed via capture, neutering, return or adoption. The document also said eligible animal-protection groups could receive support through government service purchases and public-interest programs. Back in Chongqing, Jian explained that relying entirely on subsidies, donations or unpaid work would not be sustainable. "Only by using commercial operations to support rescue can we keep this going in the long run," she said. During Chongqing's hot summer, the park stays open until midnight. As temperatures fall in the evening, visitors arrive to see the cats and enjoy the riverside night view. Many simply sit and wait. "Here, you don't have to talk or please anyone," Jian said. "You can just sit on the steps, and maybe a cat will come over, rub against you or fall asleep in your lap." ■

The lightweight, easy-to-use devices sense body movements, providing uphill assistance and downhill cushioning to protect knees and reduce leg strain. item.title: Trio win Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels, optogenetics
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 5, 2026. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Nobel Assembly at Sweden's Karolinska Institute announced. (Xinhua/Lyu You) STOCKHOLM, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Three scientists have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the prize on Monday for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Nobel Assembly at Sweden's Karolinska Institute announced. According to the institute, optogenetics is a method that shows how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviors in the living brain. "Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered a remarkable protein, channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga. Karl Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. The laureates have laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience," the institute said in a press release. Karl Deisseroth, born in the United States, is a professor at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University. Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, both born in Germany, are professors at Humboldt University of Berlin and the University of Würzburg, respectively. The laureates will share a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (about 1.19 million U.S. dollars). ■

item.title: UN official highlights GDI's role in advancing sustainable development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
by Ada Zhang UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Five years after China proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI), its focus is shifting increasingly towards practical cooperation that addresses the priorities of developing countries, a senior UN official has said. "Five years on, the Global Development Initiative is showing how shared ambition can translate into practical support for development," Dima Al-Khatib, director of the United Nations Office for South-South Cooperation (UNOSSC), told Xinhua in a written interview. The initiative, she said, has "provided a platform for mobilizing partnerships, knowledge and resources in support of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development." According to a United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) China publication, more than 600 projects under the Global Development Project Pool had been implemented or were in progress by the end of 2024. The associated Global Development Capital Pool had mobilized 14 billion U.S. dollars in financing commitments as of March 2025. "These mechanisms illustrate how cooperation under the GDI is supporting development financing and implementation," Al-Khatib said. Al-Khatib pointed to China's longstanding cooperation with UNOSSC, which spans more than two decades. "The strength of South-South cooperation lies in helping countries turn each other's experience into solutions that work for their own communities," she said. One example is the Global South-South Development Center Project, which entered its second phase in 2025 under the China-United Nations Global South-South Development Facility. Working with the China International Center for Economic and Technical Exchanges, the project aims to strengthen a network of more than 60 technical institutions to facilitate cooperation among developing countries. In West Africa, a rice initiative involving the World Food Programme, the African Union and other partners combines technology and training to improve agricultural productivity, reduce post-harvest losses and support rural livelihoods. She also highlighted cooperation on digital development, including e-commerce training that reached participants from more than 90 countries, followed by field studies in China for policymakers from 22 developing countries. With just four years left to meet the 2030 deadline, Al-Khatib said the GDI can support accelerated Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) implementation by connecting nationally identified priorities with technologies, technical expertise, financing and capacity development. In September 2025, China and the United Nations announced the China-UN Global South-South Development Facility, with 10 million dollars in budget support for the 2025-2030 period. Established under the United Nations Fund for South-South Cooperation, the facility supports cooperation under the GDI in areas, including agriculture, technology and digital development, according to UNOSSC. Al-Khatib said the facility's first call for proposals, which concluded in August, attracted 107 proposals from 16 UN agencies and entities, covering 115 countries across the Global South. "The next phase may prioritize country ownership, measurable results and the adaptation and scaling of solutions suited to local circumstances," she said. Looking ahead, Al-Khatib emphasized the importance of aligning cooperation with the SDGs, UN social and environmental standards, and UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. "The objective is to enable developing countries to adapt, co-create and sustain solutions, and share their experience across the Global South, guided by the commitment to leave no one behind," she said. ■

item.title: Chinese military expels Philippine aircraft from Huangyan Dao airspace
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Southern Theater Command on Saturday expelled a Philippine C-208 aircraft that illegally intruded into the territorial airspace over China's Huangyan Dao without approval from the Chinese government, a spokesperson said Monday. Zhai Shichen, spokesperson for the PLA Southern Theater Command, said the command dispatched naval and air forces to track and monitor the aircraft and issued warnings to expel it in accordance with laws and regulations. Huangyan Dao is China's inherent territory, and acts by the Philippine side seriously violate China's sovereignty and are highly likely to cause unintended maritime and air incidents, Zhai said. "We sternly warn the Philippine side to stop rights violations and provocative acts immediately," Zhai said, adding that forces of the theater command remain on high alert at all times to firmly safeguard national sovereignty and security as well as regional peace and stability. ■

item.title: Global businesses eye opportunities as China import expo nears
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
SHANGHAI, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- With one month to go before the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE), companies from around the world are preparing to gather in Shanghai in east China, bringing products ranging from advanced manufacturing equipment and medical technologies to African coffee and Syrian soap. The annual expo, the world's first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports, has become a major platform for foreign companies seeking access to the vast consumer and industrial markets of the world's second-largest economy. Since its launch in 2018, the CIIE has drawn participants from more than 180 countries, regions and international organizations. Overseas exhibitors have made about 27,000 appearances at its business exhibitions, with over 3,400 new products, technologies and services making their debuts. This year's event, scheduled from Nov. 5 to 10, comes as China begins its 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) with a renewed push for high-standard opening up and stronger domestic demand. For some companies, this year's CIIE will be their first. Austria's WFL Millturn Technologies, a machine tool manufacturer that entered the Chinese market more than 20 years ago, shipped its exhibits from the industrial city of Linz in August. WFL Managing Director Stefan Hackl said the company decided to join the CIIE given China's role at the heart of the global manufacturing chain, and hopes to use the expo to expand further in the Chinese and Asia-Pacific markets. "I don't see any good reason why we will not be successful in China in the upcoming decades," Hackl said. Singapore-based Perennial Holdings Private Limited is another newcomer. The company has established China's first wholly foreign-owned tertiary general hospital in Tianjin in northern China. Since opening, the hospital has received patients from more than 40 countries and regions, while the company is pursuing further healthcare investments in more Chinese cities. "When you invest in China, you are investing in the most competitive market in the world," said Pua Seck Guan, executive chairman and CEO of Perennial Holdings. Pua added that China's opening up of its healthcare sector could create more opportunities for foreign investors. The newcomers arrive as China continues to widen market access for foreign businesses. In 2025, the country registered 70,392 newly established foreign-invested firms, a record high and up 19.1 percent year on year. In the first half of 2026, the number rose 5.3 percent from a year earlier, with foreign direct investment in actual use reaching 402.14 billion yuan (roughly 59.71 billion U.S. dollars). China is also seeking to expand imports as it works to boost domestic consumption and pursue more balanced trade. In August, imports increased by 21.7 percent, with growth exceeding that of exports for a sixth successive month. The opportunities offered by the CIIE extend beyond large multinational companies. Nearly 13,000 overseas micro, small and medium-sized enterprises have participated in the first eight editions. Syrian businessman Muhannad Shakally is preparing for his 9th CIIE. When he brought traditional Syrian soap to the inaugural expo in 2018, he was testing the Chinese market. Today, monthly orders exceed five tonnes, equivalent to around 20,000 bars. "They sell almost as soon as they arrive. I don't even keep inventory," he said. This year, he plans to introduce aromatherapy products and Syrian herbal teas, hoping to bring more products from his country to Chinese consumers. For years, the CIIE has provided free booths to exhibitors from the world's least developed countries. This year, organizers will upgrade a dedicated section for Asian and African products, with measures to help African businesses tap opportunities created by China's zero-tariff policy. Since May 1, China has applied zero-tariff treatment to imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, while expanding market access through measures including upgraded "green channels" for products such as dried chilies, coffee beans, cashews and wild aquatic items. An official delegation from Cote d'Ivoire will make its first appearance at the CIIE's business exhibition, showcasing cocoa, coffee, cashews and kola nuts. "We are very happy to participate for the first time. This will be a good opportunity to showcase Cote d'Ivoire to the world," said Rami Koné, an official with the country's export agency. Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Center for International Governance Innovation, said small and medium-sized enterprises from the Global South, particularly those in Africa, were once on the margins of global trade. China, he said, has provided them with opportunities to share in the benefits of its opening up and development. ■

item.title: Longer trips, richer experiences: China's National Day holiday reveals shifting tourism trends
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Five days into China's week-long National Day holiday, millions are still immersed in the sights, sounds and flavors of the season -- traveling, dining, exploring and enjoying the break. Yet this year, the scenes are subtly different. Travelers have ventured farther as the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday fell just three days before the National Day holiday, while family trips and experience-oriented travel are on the rise, according to travel agencies. "It points to a fundamental shift in the logic of tourism consumption, as travelers focus more on the quality of time and the richness of their experiences," said Bu Xiting, a researcher with the Communication University of China. LONGER BREAKS, RICHER CHOICES Data from Chinese online travel platform Tuniu shows that tours of 10 days or more are particularly popular during this holiday period, accounting for 26 percent of bookings. Yuan You, an internet company employee, spent three days of her 13-day break in Jiuzhaigou, southwest China's Sichuan Province, before heading to the provincial capital Chengdu for woodworking classes. "The holiday is rich while maintaining a relaxed pace," she said. Authorities across the country have rolled out a wide range of activities, consumer vouchers and subsidies to spur holiday spending. Shanghai, for example, has launched about 200 major consumption events, backed by consumer vouchers worth roughly 100 million yuan (around 14.85 million U.S. dollars). The offerings range from watching films and dining to purchasing digital products and cars, encouraging consumers to explore a broader spectrum of spending experiences. Cultural institutions, too, are broadening the ways people can experience and consume culture. The Sichuan Museum extended its holiday hours and launched a themed night tour, while Beijing's Zhongshan Park brought museums, cultural institutions and innovative brands together to create a market street featuring culture-inspired products. As more new energy vehicles hit the roads during the holiday, authorities have taken measures to ensure adequate charging facilities and convenient services. During last year's eight-day Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, Chinese travelers made 888 million domestic trips and spent a combined 809 billion yuan, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. This year, data shows that foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively, from Oct. 1 to 3. RED TOURISM, ROBOTS AND RURAL EXPERIENCES As China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. In Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, a street has staged special activities including performances of songs from the revolutionary years and a large-scale bonfire gathering. Visitor numbers on the first day of the holiday rose about 20 percent year on year. The holiday has also turned some of China's newest robots into part of the consumer experience, putting embodied intelligence to work alongside traditional culture in tourist attractions, shopping districts and ancient towns. At a cultural district in Chengdu, robots performed dances inspired by local opera's face-changing art and used digital technology to recreate tanghua, a traditional form of sugar painting. On Chunxi Road, a humanoid robot has gone beyond entertainment to take on the role of a store manager, greeting customers and recommending products rather than simply performing for them. China's growing network of robot training bases is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor -- and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference. Years of efforts to restore the environment and revitalize rural areas are also paying off. On a ridge overlooking the Miyun Reservoir in Beijing, visitors can hike to a viewing platform and enjoy outdoor concerts amid the pine trees. With roads, infrastructure and public services extending deeper into the countryside, some once-remote villages are emerging as new destinations for holidaymakers. Caijiagou, a former impoverished hillside village in east China's Shandong Province, has transformed into an art-themed destination, with murals adorning residential walls. Village official Liang Yunhui said the village has repurposed idle rural homes into cultural spaces such as an art gallery and a musical instrument museum, while hosting events featuring traditional crafts, cultural fairs and folk music. "In total, we have received more than 500,000 visits over the years," he said. On travel platform Fliggy, the number of users purchasing travel products featuring natural scenery and villages surged by nearly 50 percent from the same holiday period last year. "More travelers are seeking immersive experiences, from sampling local cuisine and making intangible cultural heritage crafts to watching distinctive performances, allowing them to gain a deeper appreciation of local culture," said a manager with Tuniu. CHINA HAUL While many Chinese tourists are venturing farther around the world, more international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. Tennis star Novak Djokovic, in Beijing for the China Open, was seen trying his hand at Chinese calligraphy at the Summer Palace, a former imperial garden. After a match, he used a traditional Chinese seal to put his mark on fans' keepsakes instead of signing autographs. Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, has become a magnet for foreign shoppers looking to experience China's tech scene firsthand. Bryan Lamothe-Arice from the United States was browsing smart devices. "I'm particularly interested in the electric bikes and all kinds of flying devices here. I'm going to tell my friends to come here. There are tech products everywhere." China's border crossings are expected to see about 2.15 million passenger trips a day on average during the National Day holiday, according to the National Immigration Administration. That growing international interest is also showing up in spending. Overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan in China in the first seven months of 2026, up 27.8 percent year on year, according to the commerce ministry. ■

item.title: China's holiday consumption market posts steady growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Consumer spending across China is holding steady midway through the seven-day National Day holiday, with early data pointing to stable growth that reflects the economy's underlying vitality. In the first three days of the holiday from Oct. 1 to 3, foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively. Notably, the government's consumer goods trade-in program drove 19.63 billion yuan (about 2.91 billion U.S. dollars) in sales over the same period, benefiting 3.48 million consumers. In breakdown, the program drove trade-ins of 46,000 vehicles, generating 7.45 billion yuan in new car sales, along with 1.51 million home appliances worth 6.5 billion yuan and 1.71 million digital and smart devices worth 4.9 billion yuan. The National Day holiday has long been one of China's peak periods for travel, tourism and spending. Authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips in total over the seven days, averaging 300 million a day. Previous data have suggested demand remains strong as railway passenger trips on Oct. 1 alone reached 25.2 million, a single-day record. To meet surging demand, China has added train services on busy routes and waived highway tolls for private cars during the holiday. Moreover, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism launched a month-long national tourism promotion campaign in late September. Local governments are hosting more than 20,000 events spanning scenic trips, autumn outings, red tourism, study tours, night activities and local food to boost diverse premium tourism offerings, while also handing out some 310 million yuan in consumer vouchers and subsidies over the month as a way to spur tourism consumption. ■

item.title: China's new generation shines at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
* China reaffirmed its continental dominance by topping the gold medal table for a record 12th straight Asian Games, securing 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals - its best-ever haul at an overseas Asiad. * The Games signaled a changing of the guard, with 548 of China's 815 athletes making their Asiad debuts and over a quarter born in 2005 or later. * Beyond traditional disciplines, young Chinese athletes broke new ground in skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle-sports aligned with the Olympic program's youth-oriented shift. NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to a close Sunday, with China topping the gold medal table for the 12th consecutive edition, and finishing with 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, its best haul at an overseas Asiad. Beyond the medal count, the Games offered a glimpse of the next generation of Chinese athletes. Young competitors rose up across a spectrum of sports -- strengthening China's traditional powerhouses, breaking new ground in emerging disciplines and signaling ambitions that extend well beyond Nagoya. DEPTH ON DISPLAY China's dominance in its traditional strength events was evident throughout the Games. Diving once again provided the clearest example. With Lian Junjie winning the men's 10m platform title, China swept all 10 diving gold medals on offer at the Games. Since making its Asiad debut in 1974, China has never missed out on a diving gold medal, and the latest title was the team's 100th diving gold in Asian Games history. That dominance extended across the water. Chinese swimmers won 30 gold, 13 silver and 11 bronze medals, their best-ever haul at the Games. They also swept all seven relay titles for the first time, while setting five Asian records and 17 Games records. On the track and field, China continued to turn depth into medals. The team won 17 gold, 14 silver and eight bronze medals, its best show at an Asiad held outside China since Bangkok 1998, to finish atop the athletics medal table. The momentum also extended to other medal-rich events. China claimed 16 of the overall 28 shooting titles and set five world records. "The Asiad gave us an opportunity to test our preparations for Los Angeles 2028," said Wang Lian, an official with China's shooting and archery administration. "It was also an important step in developing our team, particularly our promising young athletes." Weightlifting and gymnastics further underscored China's strength in established events. Yang Liuyue broke world records in the snatch and total in the women's 61kg category, while the men's gymnastics team captured its 13th consecutive Games title and the women's team extended its winning streak to 14 editions. YOUTH TAKES FLIGHT China's delegation had a distinctly youthful look at the Asiad. Of its 815 athletes, 548 were making their Asian Games debuts, while 27 percent were born in 2005 or later. In the women's 400m individual medley, 13-year-old Yu Zidi and 15-year-old Ke Wenxi took gold and silver. Yu won three golds, setting Asian Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley, as well as an Asian record in the 200m individual medley. Her performances earned her the women's Most Valuable Player award, announced by the Olympic Council of Asia on Sunday. They arrived with talent, but talent alone was not enough. Behind their breakthroughs were years of repetition, training and persistence. "Only I know how much I went through this year. But I got through it all. I hope I can keep getting better and better," Yu said. 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo won seven gold medals, the most of any athlete at the Games. His celebration of counting the golds on his fingers in the pool became one of the memorable images. That confidence was on display in the field, too. 18-year-old javelin thrower Yan Ziyi made an immediate impact, launching 70.46 meters with her first attempt to improve the Games record by 4.37 meters. "I plan to save my chance to break the world record for the 2027 World Championships in Beijing," Yan said. The emergence of young athletes such as teenage sprinter Chen Yujie offers a glimpse of what could lie ahead for Asian athletics. The 17-year-old competed in four events and won three golds and a silver, including a gold in the women's 100m in a Games-record 11.06 seconds. Off the track, her confidence was just as striking. A photo that she took a nap in the athletes' lounge before the final became a hit on Chinese social media. "These Asian Games have given me a lot of motivation. Now that it's over, I'm already looking ahead to the next challenge," Chen said. "I hope that one day I can represent China and Asian women on the world stage and showcase our strength at the Olympics." BREAKING NEW GROUND Young athletes are opening up new possibilities for Chinese sports. After years of struggling to regain the footing, China's men's football team beat Uzbekistan in a penalty shootout on Saturday to win a bronze medal, its first in 28 years at the Games. The result gave Chinese fans something more to celebrate during the National Day holiday. "This is the most valuable medal of my career," said 21-year-old center back Peng Xiao. "But I would rather see it as a starting point. I hope the generation that comes after us can one day stand higher on the podium." As the Olympic program embraces younger, more urban sports, skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle have become regular features at the Asian Games. Chinese athletes are making their mark in these events, chasing results while gaining recognition on the world stage. China's climbers made their presence felt on National Day, sweeping the women's boulder and men's speed titles to claim the country's first Asian Games gold medals in Olympic events. With Olympic and world champions in the field, both victories were hard-earned. For 17-year-old Yang Siqi, reaching the Asiad surfing final and winning women's shortboard silver turned what once seemed out of reach into reality. The teenager from the mountainous region of southwestern China secured the country's first Asian Games surfing medal. Her dedication in training even caught the attention of Song Min, a coach with South Korea's surfing team, who said he believed Yang could one day make it to the Olympics. "I have never been afraid of surfing since I first started," Yang said. "The next step is to keep improving, one step at a time." China's skateboarders also came out on top against the host nation Japan, taking gold and bronze in the women's street event with composed performances when it mattered most. 21-year-old Sun Sibei made history by winning China's first gold in the cycling BMX freestyle, which made its Asian Games debut. "I hope this niche sport can reach a wider audience, so more people can see the twists and turns in the air, and more children can have the chance to try BMX at facilities close to home," Sun said. The younger athletes are telling a different story, a story of confidence, exploration and willingness to step into unfamiliar territory. To some extent, these Games left behind more than medals: they opened up a new path for Chinese sport. ■
